t1.body: Students are only discoverable if they turn it on, and can turn it off any time.

t2.body: Professors never see a student's email until the student applies or accepts an invitation.

t3.title: No protected traits
t3.body: Names, schools, gender, nationality and similar traits are never used to score anyone.

t4.title: Reasons, not black boxes
t4.body: Every score shows what matched and what didn't, so you can disagree with it.

faq.title: Common questions
faq.q1: Is the score a prediction that I'll get the position?
faq.a1: No. It is a guide to fit, not a prediction. Many things affect real decisions — timing, funding and other applicants.
faq.q2: What does the AI actually do?
faq.a2: First we compute a transparent score from the signals above. Then an AI reviewer looks at the top results, refines the ranking and writes the explanations. If AI isn't available, you still get the transparent score.
faq.q3: Can I use AI Match without a profile?
faq.a3: You can run it, but results improve a lot with a fuller profile. We show you what's missing.

faq.title: Questions, answered
faq.q1: Where does the researcher data come from?
faq.a1: From OpenAlex, an open catalogue of the world's scholarly work. We only show people and papers that exist in that record. We never invent professors or publications.
faq.q2: Will Labora write my email for me?
faq.a2: No — on purpose. Professors can tell, and replies go to students who sound like themselves. Labora finds who to write to, explains their work, and gives specific feedback on your own draft.
faq.a3: We compare your skills, interests, experience, availability and working style with positions, labs and researchers, then explain every match. An AI reviewer refines the top results. We never use names, schools, gender, nationality or other protected traits.
faq.a4: Nobody, unless you turn on discoverability. Then only verified professors can see your profile — never your email. They can invite you, and you decide whether to reply.
faq.q5: Do professors have to be on Labora?
faq.a5: No. You can find and contact researchers anywhere in the scholarly record. Professors who join can post positions, share their research and find students.
faq.a6: Searching is free, and a free account includes a taste of summaries, email checks and AI matching. Passes unlock unlimited use — see Pricing.

emailChecker.subtitle: Paste your draft and see exactly which phrases make professors stop reading. We never rewrite your email — you keep your own voice.
emailChecker.subject: Subject line
emailChecker.subjectPlaceholder: e.g. Question about your depth-estimation paper
emailChecker.emptyBody: Write or paste an email on the left, then press “Check my email”.
emailChecker.noIssues: Nothing to fix — this reads well.
emailChecker.soundsGenericHint: How easily this email could be sent unchanged to any professor.
emailChecker.englishOnly: Phrase checks currently run on English emails. Length and structure checks still apply.
emailChecker.signInTitle: Sign in to check your email
emailChecker.signInBody: Free accounts include one check. Passes unlock unlimited checks.
emailChecker.limitBody: Passes unlock unlimited email checks, the email finder and unlimited summaries.
emailChecker.noRewrite: We point out problems but never write the email for you — professors reply to students who sound like themselves.
emailChecker.sampleBody:
Dear Sir,

I am a highly motivated and passionate student. I found your work fascinating and groundbreaking!! I would love to learn from you and your research aligns perfectly with my interests. I hope this email finds you well.

Sincerely,
Alex

gradeDesc.excellent: Specific, concise and clear. Send it.
gradeDesc.good: A solid draft — a couple of quick fixes will help.
gradeDesc.needs_work: Several things could get this ignored. Fix the red items first.
gradeDesc.risky: This is likely to be deleted. Rework it before sending.

flattery.title: Flattery
flattery.tip: Professors hear “groundbreaking” daily. Name the specific result or method that caught your attention instead.

generic_phrase.title: Generic phrase
generic_phrase.tip: Lines like “highly motivated” could describe anyone. Show it with something you have actually done.

ai_sounding.title: Sounds machine-written
ai_sounding.tip: This phrase is common in AI-generated text. Say it the way you would say it out loud.

bad_salutation.title: Impersonal greeting
bad_salutation.tip: “Dear Sir” signals a mass email. Use “Dear Professor [Last name]” — check the spelling.

informal.title: Too informal
informal.tip: Keep the tone friendly but professional — avoid text-speak and abbreviations.

missing_name.title: Greeting has no name
missing_name.tip: Address the professor by name: “Dear Professor Rivera,”.

name_not_mentioned.title: Professor's name not used
name_not_mentioned.tip: Make sure the email is clearly addressed to this specific person.

no_specific_reference.title: Doesn't reference their work
no_specific_reference.tip: Mention a specific paper, method or finding from this professor — and ask something it made you wonder.

low_specificity.title: Nothing specific
low_specificity.tip: Nothing here couldn't be sent to any professor. Add a paper, a year, a result or a concrete question.

no_own_work.title: Shows nothing you've done
no_own_work.tip: Add one concrete thing you have built, analysed, read or taken — even a small project.

no_clear_ask.title: No clear ask
no_clear_ask.tip: Say exactly what you're asking for: a conversation, a volunteer role, or a pointer to someone else.

no_signoff.title: No sign-off
no_signoff.tip: End with a short thank-you and your full name.

exclamation.title: Too many exclamation marks
exclamation.tip: One is fine; two or more reads as over-excited. Let the content carry the enthusiasm.

emoji.title: Emoji
emoji.tip: Skip emoji in a first email to a professor.

all_caps.title: ALL CAPS
all_caps.tip: Capitalised words read as shouting. Use normal case.

too_short.title: Too short
too_short.tip: Under about 45 words rarely says enough. Add what you've done and what you're asking.

too_long.title: Too long
too_long.tip: Aim for 90–180 words. Cut background that the professor doesn't need to decide.

wall_of_text.title: Wall of text
wall_of_text.tip: Break it into 2–3 short paragraphs so it can be skimmed.

no_subject.title: No subject line
no_subject.tip: A clear subject helps it get opened: mention the topic or paper.

subject_generic.title: Generic subject
subject_generic.tip: “Research” could be anything. Try naming the paper or topic you're writing about.

subject_short.title: Subject too short
subject_short.tip: Add a few words of context so the professor knows what it's about.

subject_shouty.title: Shouty subject
subject_shouty.tip: Avoid capitals and words like “urgent” — they look like spam.

strengthLabels.redirect_offer: Gives them an easy way to redirect you

followUp.title: Follow-up planner
followUp.subtitle: No reply yet? Paste the email you sent and get two well-timed follow-ups that sound like you.
followUp.subject: Original subject line
followUp.editHint: Edit freely — these are drafts to make your own.
followUp.emptyBody: Two follow-ups, spaced so you stay on their radar without being a nuisance.
followUp.tip1: Avoid finals weeks, grant deadlines and holidays.
followUp.tip2: Send early in the morning on a weekday.
followUp.tip3: After two follow-ups, move on — and ask for a redirect.
followUp.signInTitle: Sign in to plan your follow-ups
followUp.limitTitle: You've used your free follow-up plan

framework.title: The cold-email framework
framework.subtitle: A fill-in-the-blank structure built on what makes professors reply. Tap any bracket for guidance.
framework.tapHint: Tap a bracket to see how to fill it in.
framework.redFlagsSub: These signal that you haven't done your homework. Swap them for something specific.

b1.label: SPECIFIC TOPIC
b1.tip: Name the exact area, method or question — not the whole field. “Sleep-dependent memory consolidation” beats “neuroscience”.

b2.label: SPECIFIC FINDING OR QUOTE
b2.tip: Point to a real result, figure or sentence in one of their recent papers. This is the line that proves you read it.

b3.label: YOUR RESEARCH ANGLE
b3.tip: Connect it to something you've done or want to explore — a course, a dataset, a project.

b4.label: ONE GENUINE PERSONAL REASON
b4.tip: One honest sentence about why it matters to you. Keep it short and true.

b5.label: INTELLIGENT QUESTION THAT SHOWS YOU READ IT
b5.tip: Ask something the paper made you wonder — a limitation, an extension, a dataset. Avoid “tell me more about your research”.

rf1.phrase: I found your work fascinating and groundbreaking
rf1.instead: Name the specific finding that caught your attention.

rf2.phrase: I am a highly motivated student
rf2.instead: Show motivation through what you have done.

rf3.phrase: Your research aligns perfectly with my interests

rf4.phrase: I would love to learn from you
rf4.why: It makes the email about you, not their work.
rf4.instead: Ask about a specific part of their research.

rf5.phrase: I am passionate about this field
rf5.instead: Describe what you've actually done in the field.

examples.title: Emails that work — annotated
examples.subtitle: Three illustrative emails we wrote to show the patterns that earn replies. Read the notes beside each line.
examples.disclaimer: These are illustrative examples written by the Labora team, not real correspondence. Names and details are fictional.

e1.label: First-year, self-taught
e1.note1: Leads with your own interest and a real skill, then connects it to their work.
e1.note2: A specific question that could only come from reading the paper.
e1.note3: A direct ask with a low bar — and a redirect that turns “no” into a lead.

e2.label: Junior with a side project
e2.note1: Shows a project you're already working on — proof of hands-on interest.
e2.note2: Technical depth: the question shows you understood the method, not just the abstract.
e2.note3: A timeline (this summer) and an offer to help even as a volunteer.

e3.label: Humanities / social science
e3.note1: Grounds the request in a course you took and a source you read.
e3.note2: Asks about the reasoning behind a choice, not for a summary.
e3.note3: Offers something concrete: a few hours a week of archival coding.
